sources.title: Glaze fault quick reference
sources.scope: Quick reference card for glaze faults
sources.when_to_use: one-line fixes; quick reference card
sources.text:
Glaze fault quick reference
Crawling: clean the bisque, thinner coat. Pinholes: hotter bisque or a soak. Crazing: change the recipe; refiring will not help.

sources.title: Mixing a glaze batch
sources.scope: Mixing a glaze batch from dry materials
sources.when_to_use: weighing out a recipe; sieving; how much water to add; specific gravity
sources.text:
Mixing a glaze batch
Put the water in the bucket first, then the powders, so nothing cakes on the bottom. Leave it to slake for twenty minutes before stirring. Pass twice through an 80 mesh sieve. Adjust to 1.45 on the hydrometer for dipping. Write the date and the recipe code on the lid and on the side.

sources.title: Glazing by dipping
sources.scope: Applying glaze by dipping and pouring
sources.when_to_use: how thick to coat bisque; glaze running; bare patches; wax on the foot ring
sources.text:
Glazing by dipping
Wax the foot ring and let it dry. Hold with tongs, dip for a count of three and lift out with a twist to shed the drip. The coat should be the thickness of a postcard: scratch through with a pin to check. Touch up tong marks with a brush once the surface has lost its shine. Sponge the foot clean before the piece goes on a board.

sources.title: Glazing by spraying
sources.scope: Applying glaze with the spray gun
sources.when_to_use: how thick to coat bisque; spray booth; uneven coat; large pieces
sources.text:
Glazing by spraying
Thin the glaze to 1.35 on the hydrometer and strain it into the cup. Run the extractor before picking up the gun. Work on a banding wheel, keep the nozzle a forearm away and build three light passes rather than one wet one. The surface should look like fine velvet; if it glistens, stop and let it dry.

sources.title: Glaze faults
sources.scope: Diagnosing glaze faults: crawling, pinholes and crazing
sources.when_to_use: glaze pulled away from the pot; small holes in the fired surface; fine cracks in the glaze
sources.text:
Glaze faults
Crawling comes from dust or grease on the bisque, or a coat put on too thick that cracked as it dried. Wash bisque that has sat on a shelf for more than a week. Pinholes are gas still leaving the body: bisque hotter or add a soak at peak. Crazing is a fit problem between glaze and body and will not be cured by refiring; change the recipe.

sources.title: Storing glaze materials
sources.scope: Storing and labelling glaze materials
sources.when_to_use: unlabelled bucket; how long mixed glaze keeps; glaze settled hard at the bottom
sources.text:
Storing glaze materials
Every container carries the recipe code, the date and the mixer's initials on both lid and side. Anything unmarked goes to the quarantine shelf and is not used. A wet batch keeps for a year if the lid is tight. If it has hard-panned, add a teaspoon of Epsom salt solution and sieve again.

sources.title: Bisque firing schedule
sources.scope: Bisque firing schedule for greenware in the electric kiln
sources.when_to_use: first firing of unglazed pots; how fast to heat raw clay; ramp rate before glazing
sources.not_for: booking; access; fees; raku; glass; porcelain
sources.text:
Bisque firing schedule
Load bone-dry ware only. Climb 100 C per hour to 600 C so chemically bound water can leave without blowing the walls out, then 150 C per hour to 1000 C, which is cone 06. Soak ten minutes. Leave the lid shut until the pyrometer reads under 100 C.

sources.title: Glaze firing schedule, cone 6, electric kiln
sources.scope: Glaze firing schedule to cone 6 in the electric kiln
sources.when_to_use: second firing; firing glazed pots; stoneware top temperature; slow cooling
sources.not_for: booking; access; fees; recipes; raku; porcelain
sources.text:
Glaze firing schedule, cone 6, electric kiln
Climb 150 C per hour to 1100 C, then 60 C per hour to 1222 C. Soak fifteen minutes. For matte surfaces drop to 950 C and hold an hour before switching off. Leave the lid shut until the pyrometer reads under 125 C.

sources.title: Glaze firing schedule, cone 6, gas kiln
sources.scope: Glaze firing schedule to cone 6 in the gas kiln with reduction
sources.when_to_use: second firing; firing glazed pots; stoneware top temperature; body reduction; damper setting
sources.not_for: booking; access; permission; training; allowed; fees; raku
sources.text:
Glaze firing schedule, cone 6, gas kiln
Light both burners on low and candle for an hour. Begin body reduction at 900 C by closing the damper to a finger's width until a soft flame shows at the spy hole. Return to neutral at 1000 C and climb to 1222 C over five hours. Finish with ten minutes of oxidation to clear the atmosphere.

sources.title: Loading the kiln
sources.scope: Loading the kiln: shelves, posts and spacing between pots
sources.when_to_use: stacking ware; how close pieces can sit; kiln wash; glazed pots touching
sources.text:
Loading the kiln
Three posts per shelf, set in the same positions on every layer so the load carries straight down. Glazed work needs a finger's width between pieces and from the elements. Bisque can touch and can nest. Brush batt wash on the upper face of each shelf only, never the underside, where flakes fall into work below.

sources.title: Witness cones
sources.scope: Placing and reading witness cones
sources.when_to_use: checking whether a firing reached temperature; bent cone; underfired or overfired load
sources.text:
Witness cones
Set a pack of three, guide, target and guard, in a pad of wadding where it can be seen through the spy hole. A good firing bends the target tip to the level of its base, leaves the guard standing and lays the guide flat. If the guard has gone over, the load ran hot: shorten the soak next time rather than lowering the set point.

sources.title: Element care
sources.scope: Inspecting and replacing kiln elements
sources.when_to_use: kiln slow to climb; kiln not reaching temperature; sagging coils; error on the controller
sources.text:
Element care
Elements age by growing an oxide skin, which raises resistance and stretches firing times. Measure each circuit with a multimeter twice a year and replace the set when resistance has risen by ten percent. Never mix old and new in one circuit. Fire new elements empty once to 1000 C to form the protective coat before any reduction materials go near them.

sources.title: Dust control
sources.scope: Controlling clay and glaze dust; silica exposure
sources.when_to_use: sweeping the studio; mask or respirator; cleaning up dry glaze
sources.text:
Dust control
Never sweep or brush dry. Wet mop the floor and sponge the benches at the end of each session. Wear a fitted P3 half-mask whenever a bag of powder is open; paper masks do not stop respirable silica. Wash aprons weekly rather than shaking them out.

sources.title: Kiln ventilation
sources.scope: Kiln ventilation and fumes during firing
sources.when_to_use: smell while firing; vent fan; staying in the room with a hot kiln
sources.text:
Kiln ventilation
Switch the extractor on before the kiln and leave it running until the pyrometer reads under 200 C. Wax burn-off and sulphur from some clays come off between 200 C and 700 C; keep the kiln room door shut and work elsewhere during that stretch. Spy hole bungs stay in after 600 C.

probe.q: how do I throw a cylinder on the wheel

retrieval.question: how do I throw a cylinder on the wheel
retrieval.reason: exactly one current page owns this question by declared scope
retrieval.text:
Wedging
Ram's head for small amounts, spiral for anything over two kilos. Thirty turns is a minimum. Cut the lump with a wire and look at the face: it should be one even colour with no holes. Wedge on canvas or bare wood, not on plaster, which chips into the clay and blows out in the kiln.

sources.title: Hot ware and burns
sources.scope: Handling hot ware and treating minor burns
sources.when_to_use: unloading a warm kiln; gloves; touched a hot shelf
sources.text:
Hot ware and burns
Use the leather gauntlets for anything over 60 C and set work down on the kiln shelf offcuts, never on a wooden bench. For a burn, twenty minutes under cool running water straight away, then cover loosely with cling film. Anything larger than a coin, or blistered, goes to the minor injuries unit.

sources.scope: Clay bodies kept in stock and their firing ranges
sources.when_to_use: which clay for cone 6; earthenware or stoneware; shrinkage; clay for sculpture
sources.text:
Clay bodies in stock
White stoneware, bag code WS, matures at cone 6 and shrinks twelve percent. Red earthenware, RE, matures at cone 04 and must never go in a cone 6 firing, where it slumps and fuses to the shelf. Grogged crank, CR, is for sculpture and large slab work and tolerates uneven drying.

sources.text:
Drying ware
Dry slowly and evenly. Turn pots onto their rims once they will hold their shape, so the base catches up with the lip. Wrap handles and joins loosely for the first day. A piece is ready when it no longer feels cool against the cheek. Thick sculpture needs two weeks, not two days.

Glaze firing schedule, cone 6, gas kiln
Light both burners on low and candle for an hour. Begin body reduction at 900 C by closing the damper to a finger's width until a soft flame shows at the spy hole. Return to neutral at 1000 C and climb to 1222 C over five hours. Finish with ten minutes of oxidation to clear the atmosphere.

sources.title: Loading the kiln
sources.scope: Loading the kiln: shelves, posts and spacing between pots
sources.when_to_use: stacking ware; how close pieces can sit; kiln wash; glazed pots touching
sources.text:
Loading the kiln
Three posts per shelf, set in the same positions on every layer so the load carries straight down. Glazed work needs a finger's width between pieces and from the elements. Bisque can touch and can nest. Brush batt wash on the upper face of each shelf only, never the underside, where flakes fall into work below.

sources.title: Witness cones
sources.scope: Placing and reading witness cones
sources.when_to_use: checking whether a firing reached temperature; bent cone; underfired or overfired load
sources.text:
Witness cones
Set a pack of three, guide, target and guard, in a pad of wadding where it can be seen through the spy hole. A good firing bends the target tip to the level of its base, leaves the guard standing and lays the guide flat. If the guard has gone over, the load ran hot: shorten the soak next time rather than lowering the set point.

sources.title: Element care
sources.scope: Inspecting and replacing kiln elements
sources.when_to_use: kiln slow to climb; kiln not reaching temperature; sagging coils; error on the controller
sources.text:
Element care
Elements age by growing an oxide skin, which raises resistance and stretches firing times. Measure each circuit with a multimeter twice a year and replace the set when resistance has risen by ten percent. Never mix old and new in one circuit. Fire new elements empty once to 1000 C to form the protective coat before any reduction materials go near them.

sources.title: Kiln ventilation
sources.scope: Kiln ventilation and fumes during firing
sources.when_to_use: smell while firing; vent fan; staying in the room with a hot kiln
sources.text:
Kiln ventilation
Switch the extractor on before the kiln and leave it running until the pyrometer reads under 200 C. Wax burn-off and sulphur from some clays come off between 200 C and 700 C; keep the kiln room door shut and work elsewhere during that stretch. Spy hole bungs stay in after 600 C.

sources.title: Hot ware and burns
sources.scope: Handling hot ware and treating minor burns
sources.when_to_use: unloading a warm kiln; gloves; touched a hot shelf
sources.text:
Hot ware and burns
Use the leather gauntlets for anything over 60 C and set work down on the kiln shelf offcuts, never on a wooden bench. For a burn, twenty minutes under cool running water straight away, then cover loosely with cling film. Anything larger than a coin, or blistered, goes to the minor injuries unit.

Reclaiming clay
Let scraps go bone dry, then slake them in a bucket of water overnight without stirring. Pour off the clear water. Wedging
Ram's head for small amounts, spiral for anything over two kilos. Thirty turns is a minimum. Cut the lump with a wire and look at the face: it should be one even colour with no holes. Wedge on canvas or bare wood, not on plaster, which chips into the clay and blows out in the kiln.

sources.text:
Clay bodies in stock
White stoneware, bag code WS, matures at cone 6 and shrinks twelve percent. Red earthenware, RE, matures at cone 04 and must never go in a cone 6 firing, where it slumps and fuses to the shelf. Grogged crank, CR, is for sculpture and large slab work and tolerates uneven drying.

sources.text:
Firing day checklist
1. Ware bone dry, or glazed feet wiped. 2. Three posts per shelf, aligned. 3. Cone pack visible through the spy hole. 4. Extractor on. 5. Programme matches the load: bisque to 1000 C, glaze to 1222 C. 6. Log the start time on the door sheet.

Glaze faults
Crawling comes from dust or grease on the bisque, or a coat put on too thick that cracked as it dried. Wash bisque that has sat on a shelf for more than a week. Pinholes are gas still leaving the body: bisque hotter or add a soak at peak. Crazing is a fit problem between glaze and body and will not be cured by refiring; change the recipe.

Drying ware
Dry slowly and evenly. Turn pots onto their rims once they will hold their shape, so the base catches up with the lip. Wrap handles and joins loosely for the first day. A piece is ready when it no longer feels cool against the cheek. Thick sculpture needs two weeks, not two days.

sources.when_to_use: one-line fixes; quick reference card
sources.text:
Glaze fault quick reference
Crawling: clean the bisque, thinner coat. Pinholes: hotter bisque or a soak. Crazing: change the recipe; refiring will not help.

sources.title: Mixing a glaze batch
sources.scope: Mixing a glaze batch from dry materials
sources.when_to_use: weighing out a recipe; sieving; how much water to add; specific gravity
sources.text:
Mixing a glaze batch
Put the water in the bucket first, then the powders, so nothing cakes on the bottom. Leave it to slake for twenty minutes before stirring. Pass twice through an 80 mesh sieve. Adjust to 1.45 on the hydrometer for dipping. Write the date and the recipe code on the lid and on the side.

sources.title: Glazing by dipping
sources.scope: Applying glaze by dipping and pouring
sources.when_to_use: how thick to coat bisque; glaze running; bare patches; wax on the foot ring
sources.text:
Glazing by dipping
Wax the foot ring and let it dry. Hold with tongs, dip for a count of three and lift out with a twist to shed the drip. The coat should be the thickness of a postcard: scratch through with a pin to check. Touch up tong marks with a brush once the surface has lost its shine. Sponge the foot clean before the piece goes on a board.

sources.title: Glazing by spraying
sources.scope: Applying glaze with the spray gun
sources.when_to_use: how thick to coat bisque; spray booth; uneven coat; large pieces
sources.text:
Glazing by spraying
Thin the glaze to 1.35 on the hydrometer and strain it into the cup. Run the extractor before picking up the gun. Work on a banding wheel, keep the nozzle a forearm away and build three light passes rather than one wet one. The surface should look like fine velvet; if it glistens, stop and let it dry.

Storing glaze materials
Every container carries the recipe code, the date and the mixer's initials on both lid and side. Anything unmarked goes to the quarantine shelf and is not used. A wet batch keeps for a year if the lid is tight. If it has hard-panned, add a teaspoon of Epsom salt solution and sieve again.

sources.text:
Mixing a glaze batch
Put the water in the bucket first, then the powders, so nothing cakes on the bottom. Leave it to slake for twenty minutes before stirring. Pass twice through an 80 mesh sieve. Adjust to 1.45 on the hydrometer for dipping. Write the date and the recipe code on the lid and on the side.

sources.title: Glazing by dipping
sources.scope: Applying glaze by dipping and pouring
sources.when_to_use: how thick to coat bisque; glaze running; bare patches; wax on the foot ring
sources.text:
Glazing by dipping
Wax the foot ring and let it dry. Hold with tongs, dip for a count of three and lift out with a twist to shed the drip. The coat should be the thickness of a postcard: scratch through with a pin to check. Touch up tong marks with a brush once the surface has lost its shine. Sponge the foot clean before the piece goes on a board.

sources.title: Glazing by spraying
sources.scope: Applying glaze with the spray gun
sources.when_to_use: how thick to coat bisque; spray booth; uneven coat; large pieces
sources.text:
Glazing by spraying
Thin the glaze to 1.35 on the hydrometer and strain it into the cup. Run the extractor before picking up the gun. Work on a banding wheel, keep the nozzle a forearm away and build three light passes rather than one wet one. The surface should look like fine velvet; if it glistens, stop and let it dry.

sources.title: Glaze faults
sources.scope: Diagnosing glaze faults: crawling, pinholes and crazing
sources.when_to_use: glaze pulled away from the pot; small holes in the fired surface; fine cracks in the glaze
sources.text:
Glaze faults
Crawling comes from dust or grease on the bisque, or a coat put on too thick that cracked as it dried. Wash bisque that has sat on a shelf for more than a week. Pinholes are gas still leaving the body: bisque hotter or add a soak at peak. Crazing is a fit problem between glaze and body and will not be cured by refiring; change the recipe.

sources.title: Bisque firing schedule
sources.scope: Bisque firing schedule for greenware in the electric kiln
sources.when_to_use: first firing of unglazed pots; how fast to heat raw clay; ramp rate before glazing
sources.not_for: booking; access; fees; raku; glass; porcelain
sources.text:
Bisque firing schedule
Load bone-dry ware only. Climb 100 C per hour to 600 C so chemically bound water can leave without blowing the walls out, then 150 C per hour to 1000 C, which is cone 06. Soak ten minutes. Leave the lid shut until the pyrometer reads under 100 C.

sources.title: Dust control
sources.scope: Controlling clay and glaze dust; silica exposure
sources.when_to_use: sweeping the studio; mask or respirator; cleaning up dry glaze
sources.text:
Dust control
Never sweep or brush dry. Wet mop the floor and sponge the benches at the end of each session. Wear a fitted P3 half-mask whenever a bag of powder is open; paper masks do not stop respirable silica. Wash aprons weekly rather than shaking them out.

sources.title: Hot ware and burns
sources.scope: Handling hot ware and treating minor burns
sources.when_to_use: unloading a warm kiln; gloves; touched a hot shelf
sources.text:
Hot ware and burns
Use the leather gauntlets for anything over 60 C and set work down on the kiln shelf offcuts, never on a wooden bench. For a burn, twenty minutes under cool running water straight away, then cover loosely with cling film. Anything larger than a coin, or blistered, goes to the minor injuries unit.

Bisque firing schedule
Load bone-dry ware only. Climb 100 C per hour to 600 C so chemically bound water can leave without blowing the walls out, then 150 C per hour to 1000 C, which is cone 06. Soak ten minutes. Leave the lid shut until the pyrometer reads under 100 C.

Glaze firing schedule, cone 6, electric kiln
Climb 150 C per hour to 1100 C, then 60 C per hour to 1222 C. Soak fifteen minutes. For matte surfaces drop to 950 C and hold an hour before switching off. Leave the lid shut until the pyrometer reads under 125 C.

sources.scope: Glaze firing schedule to cone 6 in the gas kiln with reduction

sources.not_for: booking; access; permission; training; allowed; fees; raku
sources.text:
Glaze firing schedule, cone 6, gas kiln
Light both burners on low and candle for an hour. Begin body reduction at 900 C by closing the damper to a finger's width until a soft flame shows at the spy hole. Return to neutral at 1000 C and climb to 1222 C over five hours. Finish with ten minutes of oxidation to clear the atmosphere.

sources.title: Witness cones
sources.scope: Placing and reading witness cones
sources.when_to_use: checking whether a firing reached temperature; bent cone; underfired or overfired load
sources.text:
Witness cones
Set a pack of three, guide, target and guard, in a pad of wadding where it can be seen through the spy hole. A good firing bends the target tip to the level of its base, leaves the guard standing and lays the guide flat. If the guard has gone over, the load ran hot: shorten the soak next time rather than lowering the set point.

sources.title: Element care
sources.scope: Inspecting and replacing kiln elements
sources.when_to_use: kiln slow to climb; kiln not reaching temperature; sagging coils; error on the controller
sources.text:
Element care
Elements age by growing an oxide skin, which raises resistance and stretches firing times. Measure each circuit with a multimeter twice a year and replace the set when resistance has risen by ten percent. Never mix old and new in one circuit. Fire new elements empty once to 1000 C to form the protective coat before any reduction materials go near them.

sources.title: Kiln ventilation
sources.scope: Kiln ventilation and fumes during firing
sources.when_to_use: smell while firing; vent fan; staying in the room with a hot kiln
sources.text:
Kiln ventilation
Switch the extractor on before the kiln and leave it running until the pyrometer reads under 200 C. Wax burn-off and sulphur from some clays come off between 200 C and 700 C; keep the kiln room door shut and work elsewhere during that stretch. Spy hole bungs stay in after 600 C.

sources.title: Wedging
sources.scope: Wedging clay before throwing
sources.when_to_use: air bubbles; lumpy or uneven clay; preparing a ball for the wheel
sources.text:
Wedging
Ram's head for small amounts, spiral for anything over two kilos. Thirty turns is a minimum. Cut the lump with a wire and look at the face: it should be one even colour with no holes. Wedge on canvas or bare wood, not on plaster, which chips into the clay and blows out in the kiln.

sources.title: Drying ware
sources.scope: Drying thrown and hand-built ware to bone dry
sources.when_to_use: cracks while drying; when a pot is ready for the kiln; covering with plastic; handles pulling away
sources.text:
Drying ware
Dry slowly and evenly. Turn pots onto their rims once they will hold their shape, so the base catches up with the lip. Wrap handles and joins loosely for the first day. A piece is ready when it no longer feels cool against the cheek. Thick sculpture needs two weeks, not two days.

sources.title: Clay bodies in stock
sources.scope: Clay bodies kept in stock and their firing ranges
sources.when_to_use: which clay for cone 6; earthenware or stoneware; shrinkage; clay for sculpture
sources.text:
Clay bodies in stock
White stoneware, bag code WS, matures at cone 6 and shrinks twelve percent. Red earthenware, RE, matures at cone 04 and must never go in a cone 6 firing, where it slumps and fuses to the shelf. Grogged crank, CR, is for sculpture and large slab work and tolerates uneven drying.

sources.scope: Firing day checklist assembled from the schedules and loading rules
sources.when_to_use: checklist before switching on; what to check on firing day
sources.text:
Firing day checklist
1. Ware bone dry, or glazed feet wiped. 2. Three posts per shelf, aligned. 3. Cone pack visible through the spy hole. 4. Extractor on. 5. Programme matches the load: bisque to 1000 C, glaze to 1222 C. 6. Log the start time on the door sheet.

sources.text:
Glaze fault quick reference
Crawling: clean the bisque, thinner coat. Pinholes: hotter bisque or a soak. Crazing: change the recipe; refiring will not help.

sources.title: Glazing by dipping
sources.scope: Applying glaze by dipping and pouring
sources.when_to_use: how thick to coat bisque; glaze running; bare patches; wax on the foot ring
sources.text:
Glazing by dipping
Wax the foot ring and let it dry. Hold with tongs, dip for a count of three and lift out with a twist to shed the drip. The coat should be the thickness of a postcard: scratch through with a pin to check. Touch up tong marks with a brush once the surface has lost its shine. Sponge the foot clean before the piece goes on a board.

sources.title: Glazing by spraying
sources.scope: Applying glaze with the spray gun
sources.when_to_use: how thick to coat bisque; spray booth; uneven coat; large pieces
sources.text:
Glazing by spraying
Thin the glaze to 1.35 on the hydrometer and strain it into the cup. Run the extractor before picking up the gun. Work on a banding wheel, keep the nozzle a forearm away and build three light passes rather than one wet one. The surface should look like fine velvet; if it glistens, stop and let it dry.

sources.title: Glaze faults
sources.scope: Diagnosing glaze faults: crawling, pinholes and crazing
sources.when_to_use: glaze pulled away from the pot; small holes in the fired surface; fine cracks in the glaze
sources.text:
Glaze faults
Crawling comes from dust or grease on the bisque, or a coat put on too thick that cracked as it dried. Wash bisque that has sat on a shelf for more than a week. Pinholes are gas still leaving the body: bisque hotter or add a soak at peak. Crazing is a fit problem between glaze and body and will not be cured by refiring; change the recipe.

sources.text:
Loading the kiln
Three posts per shelf, set in the same positions on every layer so the load carries straight down. Glazed work needs a finger's width between pieces and from the elements. Bisque can touch and can nest. Brush batt wash on the upper face of each shelf only, never the underside, where flakes fall into work below.

Hot ware and burns
Use the leather gauntlets for anything over 60 C and set work down on the kiln shelf offcuts, never on a wooden bench. For a burn, twenty minutes under cool running water straight away, then cover loosely with cling film. Anything larger than a coin, or blistered, goes to the minor injuries unit.
